newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-IRABU A CROWD PLEASER IN YANKEE DEBUT.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-IRABU A CROWD PLEASER IN YANKEE DEBUT.

text.p: Japanese import Hideki Irabu lived up to the hullaballoo and satisfied a sellout Yankee Stadium crowd in his major-league debut Thursday, pitching 6-2/3 innings of nine-strikeout, five-hit, two-run baseball.
"The experience was more than I dreamed of," Irabu, who had stubbornly held out for the chance to play for the World Series champion New York Yankees, said through an interpreter.
The big right-hander had some shaky moments but threw 61 strikes against 37 balls while issuing four walks in the Yankees' 10-3 rout of the Detroit Tigers.
"Impressed" was the word of the day.
"You can't help but be impressed," said manager Joe Torre. "His poise and his stuff -- bigtime for me."
"I was probably more impressed with his poise than anything else under the circumstances," said Detroit manager Buddy Bell.
"I was impressed," said Yankee catcher Joe Girardi. "There had to be a lot of pressure on him. All of Japan was watching, even if it was 8:30 a.m. in the morning."

Irabu, who showed varying speeds of fastballs along with a nasty splitter and a deceptive changeup, got plenty of offensive support. Tino Martinez's three-run homer in the third was the big blow and the Yankees batted around in two different innings.

But all eyes were on the 6-foot-4 (1.93 m), 240-pound (109 kg) Japanese hurler who came in already having met the mayor in a City Hall ceremony, dented the car of Yankee boss George Steinbrenner in a parking lot accident, and grabbed headlines for days.
The Yankees said the paid attendance of 51,901 meant that every available ticket had been sold. A sizeable number of children were admitted free in a special promotion.

It was a festive feeling at the stadium as a large contingent of Japanese turned out and some diehard Yankee fans donned Japanese-style garb to mark the occasion. On one overhang above the first deck, fans were hanging out Japanese "K" cards to mark each of Irabu's strikeouts.

If, conservatively, the 28-year-old Irabu swelled the paying crowd by 20,000, that brought him roughly 10 percent of the way towards paying off his $3.2 million annual salary in one night's ticket sales alone.

The Yankees issued some 200 credentials in addition to their normal 100-member accredited press corps, 100 or so to Japanese. The game was broadcast live in Japan during the morning rush hour and shown on 38 large screens at high-traffic public areas in several cities.

Irabu's refusal to play for the San Diego Padres, his forcing of the deal that brought him to New York and then his progress through six minor-league starts culminated in his appearance in baseball's most hallowed stadium.
"When I got up on the mound all the things I had to go through the last six months, all the ordeals went through my mind like a flashback," said Irabu, the fourth Japanese now in the big leagues.
Irabu breezed through the first two innings, facing the minimum six batters and starting each one with a strike. He threw just four balls against 18 strikes before running into trouble in the third.

He walked Curtis Pride on a strike and four straight balls, and after Raul Casanova lined a single to right to put men on first and third, Deivi Cruz worked the count full and then hit a smash to left that scored Pride. The too ardent Casanova, however, was thrown out at third on the play.
"When they scored, he was upset," said Girardi of his pitcher. "He expects perfection."
Irabu walked another batter but struck out Travis Fryman on three pitches to end the inning.

Irabu gave up another run in the fifth, yielding a full-count double to Casanova, who advanced to third on Cruz's ground-out. Brian Hunter struck out looking but Bobby Higginson then got a first-pitch RBI single for the Tigers' second run.

Later in the inning, with the bases loaded and Irabu looking a little wild, pitching coach Mel Stottlemyre walked to the mound for a long conference that included all the infielders, and told the pitcher he was rushing his delivery.
Irabu -- who had thrown eight successive balls -- then got a gift from Bob Hamelin when the designated hitter swung on the first pitch and grounded out to third, stranding three.
"I'm sure he was looking fastball -- he saw fastball but it was a splitter," Bell said.

Irabu threw just six pitches in the sixth inning, and then got the first two batters in the seventh with ease. But with his man nearing 100 pitches and the Yanks up 10-2, Torre came out to the mound to tell him his day's work was done.
"I did that basically just so the fans could show their appreciation," Torre said.

They did, giving Irabu a standing ovation as he walked to the dugout, tipping his cap. The fans called him out from the dugout for another round of cheers. Much of the crowd then headed for the exits.

Irabu signed a four-year, $12.8 million contract after the Yankees struck a deal with the Padres. San Diego had acquired his rights from Chiba Lotte of the Japanese Pacific League, which he led last year with a 2.40 earned run average.
The Yankees plan to start Irabu again Tuesday afternoon against the visiting Cleveland Indians.
